claim: India comprises much of the persisting global childhood measles mortality.
source: India comprises much of the persisting global childhood measles mortality.
evidence: Supported by citations to Black et al., 2010 and Dabbagh et al., 2017 in the Introduction section.

claim: India implemented a mass second-dose measles immunization campaign in 2010.
source: India implemented a mass second-dose measles immunization campaign in 2010.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and detailed in the Introduction with reference to government policy documents.

claim: The Million Death Study included 27,000 child deaths in 1.3 million households surveyed from 2005 to 2013.
source: We used interrupted time series and multilevel regression to quantify the campaign's impact on measles mortality using the nationally representative Million Death Study (including 27,000 child deaths in 1.3 million households surveyed from 2005 to 2013).
evidence: Direct statement of the study sample size and timeframe.

claim: 1–59 month measles mortality rates fell 27% in campaign states following launch.
source: 1–59 month measles mortality rates fell more in the campaign states following launch (27%) versus non-campaign states (11%).
evidence: Quantitative result from the study's analysis.

claim: 1–59 month measles mortality rates fell 11% in non-campaign states following launch.
source: 1–59 month measles mortality rates fell more in the campaign states following launch (27%) versus non-campaign states (11%).
evidence: Quantitative result from the study's analysis.

claim: Declines in measles mortality were steeper in girls than boys.
source: Declines were steeper in girls than boys and were specific to measles deaths.
evidence: Comparative finding from the study's stratified analysis.

claim: Declines in mortality were specific to measles deaths.
source: Declines were steeper in girls than boys and were specific to measles deaths.
evidence: Finding from comparison with control deaths (pneumonia and diarrhoea).

claim: Children living in a campaign district had lower measles mortality risk (OR 0.6, 99% CI 0.4–0.8).
source: Measles mortality risk was lower for children living in a campaign district (OR 0.6, 99% CI 0.4–0.8) or born in 2009 or later (OR 0.8, 99% CI 0.7–0.9).
evidence: Result from multilevel logistic regression analysis.

claim: Children born in 2009 or later had lower measles mortality risk (OR 0.8, 99% CI 0.7–0.9).
source: Measles mortality risk was lower for children living in a campaign district (OR 0.6, 99% CI 0.4–0.8) or born in 2009 or later (OR 0.8, 99% CI 0.7–0.9).
evidence: Result from multilevel logistic regression analysis.

claim: The campaign averted 41,000–56,000 deaths during 2010–13.
source: The campaign averted up to 41,000–56,000 deaths during 2010–13, or 39–57% of the expected deaths nationally.
evidence: Calculated estimate from interrupted time series modeling.

claim: The campaign averted 39–57% of the expected deaths nationally during 2010–13.
source: The campaign averted up to 41,000–56,000 deaths during 2010–13, or 39–57% of the expected deaths nationally.
evidence: Calculated percentage from interrupted time series modeling.

claim: Elimination of measles deaths in India is feasible.
source: Elimination of measles deaths in India is feasible.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observed drastic declines in measles mortality.

claim: Measles remains an important cause of death among under-five children.
source: Measles remains an important cause of death among under-five children (Moss, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss, 2017.

claim: Much of the persisting global burden of measles is located in Africa and Asia, notably in India.
source: Much of this persisting global burden of measles is located in Africa and Asia, notably in India (Black et al., 2010; Dabbagh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Black et al., 2010 and Dabbagh et al., 2017.

claim: There was a 90% decline in 1–59 month measles mortality rates in India from 2000 to 2015.
source: Direct estimation of cause-specific mortality documented a 90% decline in 1–59 month measles mortality rates in India from 2000 to 2015 (Fadel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fadel et al., 2017.

claim: The Government of India launched the National Rural Health Mission in 2005.
source: In 2005, the Government of India launched the National Rural Health Mission – a program geared towards improving public health infrastructure and reducing child mortality in priority states (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2005.

claim: The National Rural Health Mission was a program geared towards improving public health infrastructure and reducing child mortality in priority states.
source: In 2005, the Government of India launched the National Rural Health Mission – a program geared towards improving public health infrastructure and reducing child mortality in priority states (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2005.

claim: In 2008, the Government of India announced a policy change to introduce second-dose measles vaccine through routine immunization.
source: In 2008, the Government of India announced a policy change to introduce second-dose measles vaccine through the routine immunization (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2010.

claim: District-level mass immunization campaigns for second-dose measles vaccine were launched in 2010 in 14 target states where first-dose measles vaccination coverage was below 80%.
source: District-level mass immunization campaigns (termed supplementary immunization activities) for second-dose measles vaccine were launched in 2010 in 14 target states where first-dose measles vaccination coverage was below 80% (hereafter referred to as campaign states).
evidence: Description of the intervention implementation.

claim: The campaign prioritized immunization of children aged 9 months to 10 years in the 14 campaign states.
source: The campaign prioritized immunization of children aged 9 months to 10 years in the 14 campaign states, after which second-dose measles vaccine was provided through routine immunization.
evidence: Description of the campaign target population.

claim: The remaining 21 states with higher coverage added only second-dose measles vaccine through routine immunization.
source: The remaining 21 states with higher coverage added only second-dose measles vaccine through routine immunization (Gupta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2011.

claim: A randomized trial was not practical in the rollout of the national campaign.
source: The ideal method of evaluation, a randomized trial, was not practical in the rollout of the national campaign.
evidence: Statement about methodological constraints.

claim: Mathematical models estimate an 84% decline in measles deaths globally during 2000–2016.
source: Mathematical models estimate an 84% decline in measles deaths globally during 2000–2016, but are unable to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions (Dabbagh et al., 2017; Jha, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dabbagh et al., 2017 and Jha, 2014.

claim: Mathematical models are unable to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions.
source: Mathematical models estimate an 84% decline in measles deaths globally during 2000–2016, but are unable to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions (Dabbagh et al., 2017; Jha, 2014).
evidence: Critique of modeling approaches supported by citations.

claim: Interrupted time series is considered a robust quasi-experimental evaluation method.
source: In these scenarios, interrupted time series is considered a robust quasi-experimental evaluation method (Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care, 2017.

claim: From 2005 to 2013, the MDS captured deaths for 13,490 girls and 13,007 boys aged 1–59 months after excluding children missing cause of death (2.8%).
source: From 2005 to 2013, the MDS captured deaths for 13,490 girls and 13,007 boys aged 1–59 months after excluding children missing cause of death (2.8%).
evidence: Direct statement of study sample characteristics.

claim: Of the 1,638 measles deaths, 79% occurred in rural areas.
source: Of the 1,638 measles deaths using the definition of one or more physician coding or the family reported a measles history for the deceased, 79% occurred in rural areas, 73% in campaign states, 59% at ages 12–59 months, and 57% in girls (Table 1).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Of the 1,638 measles deaths, 73% occurred in campaign states.
source: Of the 1,638 measles deaths using the definition of one or more physician coding or the family reported a measles history for the deceased, 79% occurred in rural areas, 73% in campaign states, 59% at ages 12–59 months, and 57% in girls (Table 1).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Of the 1,638 measles deaths, 59% occurred at ages 12–59 months.
source: Of the 1,638 measles deaths using the definition of one or more physician coding or the family reported a measles history for the deceased, 79% occurred in rural areas, 73% in campaign states, 59% at ages 12–59 months, and 57% in girls (Table 1).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Of the 1,638 measles deaths, 57% occurred in girls.
source: Of the 1,638 measles deaths using the definition of one or more physician coding or the family reported a measles history for the deceased, 79% occurred in rural areas, 73% in campaign states, 59% at ages 12–59 months, and 57% in girls (Table 1).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: 76% of families reporting a measles death noted the child to have a history of measles.
source: 76% of families reporting a measles death noted the child to have a history of measles (using the local language term), but only 39% of the deceased children received at least one dose of measles vaccine.
evidence: Descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Only 39% of the deceased children received at least one dose of measles vaccine.
source: 76% of families reporting a measles death noted the child to have a history of measles (using the local language term), but only 39% of the deceased children received at least one dose of measles vaccine.
evidence: Descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: The proportion of measles deaths at 1–59 months in campaign states reporting at least one dose of measles vaccine rose from 34% to 47% from 2005–2009 to 2010–2013.
source: The proportion of measles deaths at 1–59 months in campaign states reporting at least one dose of measles vaccine rose modestly (34% to 47%) from 2005–2009 to 2010–2013, but was mostly unchanged in non-campaign states (48% to 51%).
evidence: Descriptive statistic showing temporal change.

claim: The proportion of measles deaths at 1–59 months in non-campaign states reporting at least one dose of measles vaccine was mostly unchanged (48% to 51%) from 2005–2009 to 2010–2013.
source: The proportion of measles deaths at 1–59 months in campaign states reporting at least one dose of measles vaccine rose modestly (34% to 47%) from 2005–2009 to 2010–2013, but was mostly unchanged in non-campaign states (48% to 51%).
evidence: Descriptive statistic showing temporal change.

claim: The proportion vaccinated against measles did not differ across case definitions.
source: Despite inherent misclassification that can be expected from verbal autopsies, we observed that the proportion vaccinated against measles did not differ across case definitions, suggesting that physician assignment of deaths was not unduly biased by a history of measles vaccination (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: Analysis of potential bias in case ascertainment.

claim: Physician assignment of deaths was not unduly biased by a history of measles vaccination.
source: Despite inherent misclassification that can be expected from verbal autopsies, we observed that the proportion vaccinated against measles did not differ across case definitions, suggesting that physician assignment of deaths was not unduly biased by a history of measles vaccination (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: Inference from the observation that vaccination proportions were similar across case definitions.

claim: Annual measles deaths at ages 1–59 months fell from 62,000 to 24,000 from 2005 to 2013.
source: Annual measles deaths at ages 1–59 months fell from 62,000 to 24,000 from 2005 to 2013 (Figure 1).
evidence: Quantitative result shown in Figure 1.

claim: Prior to campaign launch, 76% of measles deaths were concentrated in campaign states.
source: Prior to campaign launch, 76% of measles deaths were concentrated in campaign states, 55% of which were in the states of Uttar Pradesh (18%), Madhya Pradesh (15%), Rajasthan (11%), and Bihar (11%).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from pre-campaign period.

claim: Prior to campaign launch, 55% of measles deaths in campaign states were in the states of Uttar Pradesh (18%), Madhya Pradesh (15%), Rajasthan (11%), and Bihar (11%).
source: Prior to campaign launch, 76% of measles deaths were concentrated in campaign states, 55% of which were in the states of Uttar Pradesh (18%), Madhya Pradesh (15%), Rajasthan (11%), and Bihar (11%).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from pre-campaign period.

claim: Following campaign launch, 59% of measles deaths were in campaign states.
source: Following campaign launch, 59% of measles deaths were in campaign states, with 38% in the above four states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from post-campaign period shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Following campaign launch, 38% of measles deaths were in the states of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Bihar.
source: Following campaign launch, 59% of measles deaths were in campaign states, with 38% in the above four states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Descriptive statistic from post-campaign period shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The age distributions did not differ greatly between pre-campaign and post-campaign periods.
source: The age distributions did not differ greatly between pre-campaign and post-campaign periods (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observation from Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The average annual rate reduction (AARR) in measles mortality over the full study period was 12%.
source: The average annual rate reduction (AARR) in measles mortality over the full study period was 12% but accelerated to 22% following campaign launch.
evidence: Calculated statistic from the study data.

claim: The AARR in measles mortality accelerated to 22% following campaign launch.
source: The average annual rate reduction (AARR) in measles mortality over the full study period was 12% but accelerated to 22% following campaign launch.
evidence: Calculated statistic from the study data.

claim: Post-campaign declines in measles mortality were faster in the campaign states (27%) versus non-campaign states (11%).
source: Post-campaign declines in measles mortality were faster in the campaign states (27%) versus non-campaign states (11%).
evidence: Comparative statistic from the study data.

claim: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%).
source: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%) and in the states of Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%) (Table 2).
evidence: Statistic from Table 2.

claim: The AARR in Madhya Pradesh was 20%.
source: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%) and in the states of Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%) (Table 2).
evidence: Statistic from Table 2.

claim: The AARR in Uttar Pradesh was 19%.
source: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%) and in the states of Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%) (Table 2).
evidence: Statistic from Table 2.

claim: The AARR in Rajasthan was 17%.
source: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%) and in the states of Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%) (Table 2).
evidence: Statistic from Table 2.

claim: The AARR in Chhattisgarh was 17%.
source: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%) and in the states of Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%) (Table 2).
evidence: Statistic from Table 2.

claim: The AARR in Gujarat was 14%.
source: The AARR declined most notably in campaign states (15%) and in the states of Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%) (Table 2).
evidence: Statistic from Table 2.

claim: Measles mortality rates among 1–59 month-old children in campaign states declined significantly following campaign launch when compared to control deaths.
source: Measles mortality rates among 1–59 month-old children in campaign states declined significantly following campaign launch (Figure 2) when compared to control deaths from injuries, congenital anomalies, and non-communicable diseases of the same ages.
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: There were no other mass public health interventions targeting the 1-59 month age group during the study period.
source: There were no other mass public health interventions targeting this age group during the study period.
evidence: Statement about the absence of confounding interventions.

claim: Control deaths from injuries, congenital anomalies, and non-communicable diseases are unaffected by measles vaccination.
source: The choice of control deaths is unbiased as these conditions are unaffected by measles vaccination and provide pre-intervention trends comparable to trends of measles deaths from 2005 to 2009.
evidence: Justification for control group selection based on biological plausibility.

claim: Control deaths provide pre-intervention trends comparable to trends of measles deaths from 2005 to 2009.
source: The choice of control deaths is unbiased as these conditions are unaffected by measles vaccination and provide pre-intervention trends comparable to trends of measles deaths from 2005 to 2009.
evidence: Justification for control group selection based on statistical comparison.

claim: There was a temporary increase in measles mortality in 2009.
source: We noted a temporary increase in measles mortality in 2009.
evidence: Observation from the data.

claim: The temporary increase in measles mortality in 2009 might reflect increased reporting as this was also the period when measles surveillance expanded.
source: This might reflect increased reporting as this was also the period when measles surveillance expanded.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed increase.

claim: 2009 was used as the intervention year to account for the increased reporting.
source: Thus, we used 2009 as the intervention year to account for the increased reporting.
evidence: Methodological decision based on the observed data pattern.

claim: Prior to campaign launch, the slope of measles mortality in campaign states remained unchanged at –0.004 deaths per thousand live births (95% CI –0.065, 0.056).
source: Prior to campaign launch, the slope of measles mortality in campaign states remained unchanged at –0.004 deaths per thousand live births (95% CI –0.065, 0.056; Table 3).
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis in Table 3.

claim: Prior to campaign launch, the control deaths remained unchanged with a slope of 0.003 (95% CI –0.054, 0.062).
source: The control deaths also remained unchanged with an analogous slope of 0.003 (95% CI –0.054, 0.062).
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis.

claim: Following campaign launch, the slope of measles mortality in campaign states fell significantly to –0.164 (95% CI –0.320, –0.008, p=0.040).
source: Following campaign launch, the slope of measles mortality in campaign states fell significantly to –0.164 (95% CI –0.320, –0.008, p=0.040), whereas the slope for the control deaths remained unchanged.
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis.

claim: Following campaign launch, the slope for the control deaths remained unchanged.
source: Following campaign launch, the slope of measles mortality in campaign states fell significantly to –0.164 (95% CI –0.320, –0.008, p=0.040), whereas the slope for the control deaths remained unchanged.
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis.

claim: Declines in measles mortality in India overall were similar to declines in campaign states (–0.132, 95% CI –0.252, –0.011, p=0.034).
source: Declines in measles mortality in India overall were similar to declines in campaign states (–0.132, 95% CI –0.252, –0.011, p=0.034; Figure 3).
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Non-campaign states saw no significant change in measles mortality rates following campaign launch.
source: In comparison, non-campaign states saw no significant change in measles mortality rates following campaign launch.
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis.

claim: The rate ratio of 1–59 month measles mortality between campaign states and non-campaign states fell from 3.1 to 1.8 during 2005–2013.
source: Notably, the rate ratio of 1–59 month measles mortality between campaign states and non-campaign states fell from 3.1 to 1.8 during 2005–2013.
evidence: Calculated statistic from the study data.

claim: There were no significant changes in slope for pneumonia deaths following campaign launch.
source: The declines were specific to measles deaths, as we observed no significant changes in slope for pneumonia and diarrhoea deaths following campaign launch.
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis.

claim: There were no significant changes in slope for diarrhoea deaths following campaign launch.
source: The declines were specific to measles deaths, as we observed no significant changes in slope for pneumonia and diarrhoea deaths following campaign launch.
evidence: Result from interrupted time series analysis.

claim: Girls residing in campaign states saw steeper declines in measles mortality relative to boys.
source: Girls residing in campaign states saw steeper declines in measles mortality relative to boys, even though the direction of effect was similar in both sexes.
evidence: Result from stratified interrupted time series analysis.

claim: The direction of effect was similar in both sexes.
source: Girls residing in campaign states saw steeper declines in measles mortality relative to boys, even though the direction of effect was similar in both sexes.
evidence: Result from stratified interrupted time series analysis.

claim: In campaign states, the decline in measles mortality was significant at 12–59 months.
source: In campaign states, the decline in measles mortality was significant at 12–59 months but not significant at 1–11 months.
evidence: Result from age-stratified interrupted time series analysis.

claim: In campaign states, the decline in measles mortality was not significant at 1–11 months.
source: In campaign states, the decline in measles mortality was significant at 12–59 months but not significant at 1–11 months.
evidence: Result from age-stratified interrupted time series analysis.

claim: Alternative definitions of measles cases yielded similar results.
source: At ages 1–59 months, alternative definitions of measles cases, using one or both physicians assigning measles as the underlying cause of death, also yielded similar results (Figure 4).
evidence: Result from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: A significant change in slope and level was observed in campaign states when two physicians agreed immediately or when one physician assigned measles as the cause of death.
source: We observed a significant change in slope and level in campaign states when two physicians agreed immediately or when one physician assigned measles as the cause of death (both definitions excluded a family reported history of measles which might have been affected by publicity for the campaign).
evidence: Result from sensitivity analysis using narrower case definitions.

claim: Moving the intervention year forward to 2010 resulted in the slope of measles mortality following campaign launch becoming non-significant (–0.01, 95% CI –0.08, 0.05).
source: Moving the intervention year forward to 2010 resulted in the slope of measles mortality following campaign launch becoming non-significant (–0.01, 95% CI –0.08, 0.05).
evidence: Result from sensitivity analysis.

claim: When using 2010 as the intervention year, a significant decrease in level of measles mortality following campaign launch was observed (–1.05, 95% CI –1.50, –0.61).
source: However, we observed a significant decrease in level of measles mortality following campaign launch (–1.05, 95% CI –1.50, –0.61).
evidence: Result from sensitivity analysis.

claim: In all other stratified analyses, no significant change in level was observed.
source: In all other stratified analyses, we observed no significant change in level (Table 3).
evidence: Result from stratified analyses in Table 3.

claim: National measles immunization coverage improved from 2002 to 2014, particularly in campaign states.
source: National measles immunization coverage (defined as the percentage of children aged 12 to 23 months receiving any dose of measles vaccine from routine immunization) improved from 2002 to 2014, particularly in campaign states (Figure 5).
evidence: Result from analysis of national survey data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was a significant increase in measles vaccination coverage in the campaign states relative to non-campaign states, concurrent with campaign launch (difference-in-difference estimate 16.9%, p=0.0000009).
source: In difference-in-difference analysis, we observed a significant increase in measles vaccination coverage in the campaign states relative to non-campaign states, concurrent with campaign launch (difference-in-difference estimate 16.9%, p=0.0000009).
evidence: Result from difference-in-difference analysis.

claim: Vitamin A supplementation, pneumonia treatment-seeking, oral rehydration, maternal literacy, and diarrhoea treatment-seeking showed significant increases over time.
source: Other coverage indicators, such as vitamin A supplementation, pneumonia treatment-seeking, oral rehydration, maternal literacy, and diarrhoea treatment-seeking showed significant increases over time, but these increases did not differ significantly between campaign and other states (Figure 5).
evidence: Result from analysis of national survey data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Increases in vitamin A supplementation, pneumonia treatment-seeking, oral rehydration, maternal literacy, and diarrhoea treatment-seeking did not differ significantly between campaign and other states.
source: Other coverage indicators, such as vitamin A supplementation, pneumonia treatment-seeking, oral rehydration, maternal literacy, and diarrhoea treatment-seeking showed significant increases over time, but these increases did not differ significantly between campaign and other states (Figure 5).
evidence: Result from difference-in-difference analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The odds of measles mortality were higher at 12–59 months (OR 1.5, 99% CI 1.3–1.7) than at ages 1–11 months.
source: Among 26,505 overall child deaths at 1–59 months for the whole of India from 2005 to 2013, the odds of measles mortality were higher at 12–59 months (OR 1.5, 99% CI 1.3–1.7) than at ages 1–11 months, after adjusting for covariates identified in the above difference-in-difference analyses (Figure 6).
evidence: Result from multilevel logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Girls had higher odds of measles mortality (OR 1.3, 99% CI 1.1–1.5) than boys.
source: Girls had higher odds of measles mortality (OR 1.3, 99% CI 1.1–1.5) than boys.
evidence: Result from multilevel logistic regression analysis.

claim: Girls had higher excess measles mortality risk relative to all-cause mortality in campaign states than boys.
source: Consistent with this finding, girls had higher excess measles mortality risk relative to all-cause mortality in campaign states than boys, and the excess risk was distributed far more widely in girls than boys in these states (Figure 7).
evidence: Result from geographical analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The excess measles mortality risk was distributed far more widely in girls than boys in campaign states.
source: Consistent with this finding, girls had higher excess measles mortality risk relative to all-cause mortality in campaign states than boys, and the excess risk was distributed far more widely in girls than boys in these states (Figure 7).
evidence: Result from geographical analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The majority of deaths averted were in campaign states (median 41,000).
source: The majority of deaths averted were in campaign states (median 41,000) with a similar number of deaths averted among girls (median 18,500) and boys (median 22,500) in these states.
evidence: Calculated estimate from mortality impact analysis.

claim: A similar number of deaths were averted among girls (median 18,500) and boys (median 22,500) in campaign states.
source: The majority of deaths averted were in campaign states (median 41,000) with a similar number of deaths averted among girls (median 18,500) and boys (median 22,500) in these states.
evidence: Calculated estimate from mortality impact analysis.

claim: The measles vaccine has high efficacy, preventing infection and death in 90–95% of children who receive two doses.
source: The measles vaccine has high efficacy, preventing infection and death in 90–95% of children who receive two doses (Guerra et al., 2017; Moss, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guerra et al., 2017 and Moss, 2017.

claim: Evidence for vaccine effectiveness in low- and middle-income countries is more limited.
source: However, evidence for vaccine effectiveness in low- and middle-income countries is more limited.
evidence: Statement about the state of evidence in the literature.

claim: Direct estimates of 41,000–56,000 measles deaths averted are consistent with modeled estimates documenting approximately 66,000 under-five child deaths averted.
source: Our direct estimates of 41,000–56,000 measles deaths averted are consistent with modeled estimates documenting approximately 66,000 under-five child deaths averted (Verguet et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with published modeling study supported by citation to Verguet et al., 2017.

claim: Direct data are a far more robust form of evidence than modeled estimates.
source: However, direct data are a far more robust form of evidence.
evidence: Statement about the relative strength of different types of evidence.

claim: The study documented 24,000 measles deaths in 2013 using a broad case definition that included family reporting of history of measles.
source: We document 24,000 measles deaths in 2013 using a broad case definition that included family reporting of history of measles.
evidence: Direct statement of study finding.

claim: WHO estimated 49,000 measles deaths in 2015 using a definition of either clinician-suspected measles infection or a diagnosis of fever with rash and cough, runny nose, or red eyes.
source: WHO estimated 49,000 measles deaths in 2015 using a definition of either clinician-suspected measles infection or a diagnosis of fever with rash and cough, runny nose, or red eyes (World Health Organization, 2018a; World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2018a and World Health Organization, 2016.

claim: The addition of possible measles deaths with rash and fever to the original case definition raised the estimate of measles deaths in 2013 from 24,000 to 46,000.
source: The addition of possible measles deaths with rash and fever to our original case definition raised the estimate of measles deaths in 2013 from 24,000 to 46,000.
evidence: Result from sensitivity analysis using alternative case definition.

claim: At the observed rate of decline, 35,000 deaths would be expected in 2015 using the WHO definition.
source: At our observed rate of decline, we would expect 35,000 deaths in 2015 using the WHO definition.
evidence: Projection based on observed trends.

claim: Fadel et al. (2017) documented 7,000 measles deaths in 2015 using a narrower case definition.
source: Fadel et al. (2017) documented 7,000 measles deaths in 2015 using a narrower case definition that excluded a history of measles and where all deaths were so assigned by dual physician coding with final adjudication by a third senior physician if needed.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fadel et al., 2017.

claim: Substantial downward revisions of WHO modeled estimates are likely needed.
source: Thus, substantial downward revisions of WHO modeled estimates are likely needed.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of direct data with WHO estimates.

claim: The relationship between measles cases and deaths in India is uncertain.
source: The relationship between measles cases and deaths in India is also uncertain, given that WHO incidence estimates are inconsistent with documented case fatality rates in India which range from 0.8–1.4% (Sudfeld and Halsey, 2009; Verguet et al., 2017; Wolfson et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2016; World Health Organization, 2018b; Murhekar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple sources documenting case fatality rates.

claim: Documented case fatality rates in India range from 0.8–1.4%.
source: The relationship between measles cases and deaths in India is also uncertain, given that WHO incidence estimates are inconsistent with documented case fatality rates in India which range from 0.8–1.4% (Sudfeld and Halsey, 2009; Verguet et al., 2017; Wolfson et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2016; World Health Organization, 2018b; Murhekar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sudfeld and Halsey, 2009; Verguet et al., 2017; Wolfson et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2016; World Health Organization, 2018b; Murhekar et al., 2014.

claim: Measles elimination is challenging due to its high infectivity.
source: Measles elimination is challenging due to its high infectivity – each infected child can infect an additional 4–26 children in South-east Asia (Guerra et al., 2017; Holzmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guerra et al., 2017 and Holzmann et al., 2016.

claim: Each infected child can infect an additional 4–26 children in South-east Asia.
source: Measles elimination is challenging due to its high infectivity – each infected child can infect an additional 4–26 children in South-east Asia (Guerra et al., 2017; Holzmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guerra et al., 2017 and Holzmann et al., 2016.

claim: WHO estimated the coverage of first-dose vaccine in South-east Asia to be below the levels that would achieve herd immunity (85% in 2012).
source: The WHO estimated the coverage of first-dose vaccine in South-east Asia (which includes India) to be below the levels that would achieve herd immunity (85% in 2012) and stagnation of coverage in the past decade (Dabbagh et al., 2017; Moss, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dabbagh et al., 2017 and Moss, 2017.

claim: There has been stagnation of first-dose measles vaccine coverage in South-east Asia in the past decade.
source: The WHO estimated the coverage of first-dose vaccine in South-east Asia (which includes India) to be below the levels that would achieve herd immunity (85% in 2012) and stagnation of coverage in the past decade (Dabbagh et al., 2017; Moss, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dabbagh et al., 2017 and Moss, 2017.

claim: India remains endemic to measles given suboptimal coverage.
source: Documented measles outbreaks indicate that India remains endemic to measles given suboptimal coverage, with about 3 million infants not receiving first-dose measles vaccination in 2013 (Dabbagh et al., 2017; Jamir et al., 2016; Singh and Garg, 2017; Vaidya et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dabbagh et al., 2017; Jamir et al., 2016; Singh and Garg, 2017; Vaidya et al., 2016.

claim: About 3 million infants did not receive first-dose measles vaccination in 2013.
source: Documented measles outbreaks indicate that India remains endemic to measles given suboptimal coverage, with about 3 million infants not receiving first-dose measles vaccination in 2013 (Dabbagh et al., 2017; Jamir et al., 2016; Singh and Garg, 2017; Vaidya et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dabbagh et al., 2017; Jamir et al., 2016; Singh and Garg, 2017; Vaidya et al., 2016.

claim: India's Integrated Disease Surveillance Program reported a decline in annual measles outbreaks during 2011–2013 but gradual increases since.
source: India's Integrated Disease Surveillance Program reported a decline in annual measles outbreaks during 2011–2013 but gradual increases since (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2018.

claim: The Global Vaccine Action Plan for 2012–2020 recommends second-dose measles vaccine to achieve herd immunity at 95% coverage to eliminate measles transmission.
source: The Global Vaccine Action Plan for 2012–2020 and the Government of India recommend second-dose measles vaccine to achieve herd immunity at 95% coverage to eliminate measles transmission (Dabbagh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dabbagh et al., 2017.

claim: The Government of India recommends second-dose measles vaccine to achieve herd immunity at 95% coverage to eliminate measles transmission.
source: The Global Vaccine Action Plan for 2012–2020 and the Government of India recommend second-dose measles vaccine to achieve herd immunity at 95% coverage to eliminate measles transmission (Dabbagh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dabbagh et al., 2017.

claim: Supplementary immunization activities must be regularly scheduled to reach herd immunity and to combat resurgence.
source: Supplementary immunization activities must be regularly scheduled to reach herd immunity and to combat resurgence (Verguet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verguet et al., 2017.

claim: The observed reduction in under-five measles mortality may show herd immunity in cohorts born within nine months of the campaign launch.
source: The observed reduction in under-five measles mortality may show herd immunity in cohorts born within nine months of the campaign launch.
evidence: Inference from the observed mortality reductions.

claim: Since 2013, 11 states in India have implemented laboratory-confirmed measles surveillance.
source: Since 2013, 11 states in India have implemented laboratory-confirmed measles surveillance.
evidence: Statement about surveillance infrastructure.

claim: Laboratory-confirmed measles surveillance provides sero-epidemiological data to facilitate diagnoses of measles, detect suspected cases, and sequence circulating measles genotypes.
source: This infrastructure provides sero-epidemiological data to facilitate diagnoses of measles, detect suspected cases, and sequence circulating measles genotypes (Bose et al., 2014; Vaidya, 2015; Vaidya and Chowdhury, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bose et al., 2014; Vaidya, 2015; Vaidya and Chowdhury, 2017.

claim: The measles campaign was particularly successful for girls, which saw greater absolute declines in measles mortality than boys.
source: The measles campaign was particularly successful for girls, which saw greater absolute declines in measles mortality than boys.
evidence: Result from stratified analysis.

claim: The girl-boy gap in measles mortality rates narrowed.
source: Though the girl-boy gap in measles mortality rates narrowed, mortality remains higher in girls, as is the case for other infectious causes of death at ages 1–59 months (Fadel et al., 2017).
evidence: Result from the study data with citation to Fadel et al., 2017.

claim: Mortality remains higher in girls than boys.
source: Though the girl-boy gap in measles mortality rates narrowed, mortality remains higher in girls, as is the case for other infectious causes of death at ages 1–59 months (Fadel et al., 2017).
evidence: Result from the study data with citation to Fadel et al., 2017.

claim: Persisting higher mortality rates among girls than boys may be due to lower vaccination coverage, social preference for boys, and lower levels of breastfeeding and health care access.
source: Persisting higher mortality rates among girls than boys may be due to lower vaccination coverage, social preference for boys, and lower levels of breastfeeding and health care access (Alkema et al., 2014; Corsi et al., 2009; Fadel et al., 2017; Guilmoto et al., 2018; Jha et al., 2006b; Ram et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alkema et al., 2014; Corsi et al., 2009; Fadel et al., 2017; Guilmoto et al., 2018; Jha et al., 2006b; Ram et al., 2013.

claim: The interrupted time series design addresses potential confounding by the effects of different policies occurring at the same time as the measles campaign launch.
source: The interrupted time series design addresses potential confounding by the effects of different policies occurring at the same time as the measles campaign launch.
evidence: Statement about the methodological strength of the study design.

claim: The majority of child causes of death were declining from 2000 onward.
source: Given that the majority of child causes of death were declining from 2000 onward, we selected unbiased control deaths comparable with the pre-intervention trends of measles, pneumonia, and diarrhoea deaths.
evidence: Statement about background mortality trends.

claim: The lack of effect in pneumonia deaths may be due to measles contributing a smaller etiologic fraction than other viral, bacterial, or fungal agents.
source: The lack of effect in pneumonia deaths may be due to measles contributing a smaller etiologic fraction than other viral, bacterial, or fungal agents (Farrar et al., submitted).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation to Farrar et al., submitted.

claim: The success of the measles campaign is the increase in vaccination in campaign states to levels comparable with non-campaign states.
source: The success of the measles campaign is the increase in vaccination in campaign states to levels comparable with non-campaign states.
evidence: Inference from the coverage data analysis.

claim: The introduction of second-dose measles through routine immunization in non-campaign states contributed to the declines in measles mortality nationally.
source: Though the effect was smaller in non-campaign states, the introduction of second-dose measles through routine immunization in these non-campaign states also contributed to the declines in measles mortality nationally.
evidence: Inference from the observed mortality declines in non-campaign states.

claim: Most deaths in India occur at home and without medical attention.
source: Most deaths in India as in most low- and middle-income countries occur at home and without medical attention, precluding complete death registration and certification (Registrar General of India, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Registrar General of India, 2016.

claim: The Registrar General of India and the Centre for Global Health Research implemented the MDS in 1.3 million households within its Sample Registration System starting in 2001.
source: Starting in 2001, the Registrar General of India (RGI) and the Centre for Global Health Research implemented the MDS in 1.3 million households within its Sample Registration System (SRS), an ongoing demographic surveillance system.
evidence: Description of the study implementation.

claim: The SRS captures approximately 140,000 births and 46,000 deaths annually.
source: Over the ensuing decade, the SRS randomly selects and monitors several thousand units within these areas, capturing approximately 140,000 births and 46,000 deaths annually.
evidence: Description of the surveillance system.

claim: The MDS relies on 14,268 units drawn from the 1991 and 2001 censuses.
source: This MDS relies on 14,268 units drawn from the 1991 and 2001 censuses (Registrar General of India, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Registrar General of India, 2016.

claim: Approximately 900 trained non-medical RGI surveyors conduct two semi-annual rounds of interviews.
source: Approximately 900 trained non-medical RGI surveyors conduct two semi-annual rounds of interviews of household members or close associates of those who died in the preceding round.
evidence: Description of data collection procedures.

claim: The interview uses a modified version of the 2011 WHO verbal autopsy questionnaire.
source: The interview uses a modified version of the 2011 WHO verbal autopsy questionnaire to capture death events and their chronology through structured checklist questions about key symptoms and a local language narrative.
evidence: Description of data collection instrument.

claim: Each field report is randomly assigned to two of 404 trained physicians.
source: Each field report is randomly assigned to two of 404 trained physicians (Jha et al., 2008), who classify the underlying causes of death according to the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10; Table 5) (Jha et al., 2006a; World Health Organization, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jha et al., 2008; Jha et al., 2006a; World Health Organization, 1992.

claim: Coding differences are resolved by both physicians who anonymously receive the other's case notes.
source: Coding differences are resolved by both physicians who anonymously receive the other's case notes.
evidence: Description of quality assurance procedures.

claim: One of 40 senior physicians adjudicates persisting differences.
source: One of 40 senior physicians adjudicates persisting differences (Aleksandrowicz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aleksandrowicz et al., 2014.

claim: The campaign targeted children from 9 months to 10 years of age.
source: Though the campaign targeted children from 9 months to 10 years of age, our analysis focuses on children aged 1–59 months who comprised 84% (1638/1958) of these deaths.
evidence: Description of the campaign target population.

claim: Children aged 1–59 months comprised 84% (1638/1958) of measles deaths in the campaign target age group.
source: Though the campaign targeted children from 9 months to 10 years of age, our analysis focuses on children aged 1–59 months who comprised 84% (1638/1958) of these deaths.
evidence: Calculation from the study data.

claim: Three-year moving averages were calculated weighted by SRS sampling probabilities for the 35 Indian states or territories.
source: We applied proportions of measles deaths to all-causes among 1–59 month children and calculated three-year moving averages weighted by SRS sampling probabilities for the 35 Indian states or territories.
evidence: Description of analytical methods.

claim: Weighted proportions were applied to live births and deaths for India at the national and state level derived from SRS vital statistics and census data.
source: We applied these weighted proportions to live births and deaths for India at the national and state level (derived from SRS vital statistics and census data) and adjusted to match the national birth totals from the UN Population Division and death totals from UN Population Division's Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (Fadel et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of analytical methods with citation to Fadel et al., 2017.

claim: Rates were calculated for each six-month period as death counts were too low to separate into monthly data.
source: We calculated rates for each six-month period as death counts were too low to separate into monthly data as semi-annual rates correspond to the frequency of survey collection conducted in the MDS.
evidence: Justification for the temporal resolution of the analysis.

claim: Log transformed rates were used to account for potential nonlinearity.
source: We used log transformed rates to account for potential nonlinearity.
evidence: Description of analytical methods.

claim: The average annual rate of reduction was calculated using the linear association between log rate and time.
source: We calculated the average annual rate of reduction by India and by state using the linear association between log rate and time (UNICEF, 2007).
evidence: Description of analytical methods with citation to UNICEF, 2007.

claim: The data were fitted using ordinary least squares linear segmented regression.
source: We fitted the data using ordinary least squares linear segmented regression (Linden, 2015).
evidence: Description of analytical methods with citation to Linden, 2015.

claim: Control groups were selected by comparing their pre-intervention trends to that of measles, pneumonia, and diarrhoea.
source: We selected various control groups by comparing their pre-intervention trends to that of measles, pneumonia, and diarrhoea (Linden, 2015).
evidence: Description of analytical methods with citation to Linden, 2015.

claim: Control selection used a matching framework to match control deaths to measles, pneumonia, or diarrhoea deaths based on balancing of the pre-intervention trend characteristics.
source: Control selection used a matching framework to match control deaths to our measles, pneumonia, or diarrhoea deaths based on balancing of the pre-intervention trend characteristics (Linden, 2018).
evidence: Description of analytical methods with citation to Linden, 2018.

claim: The pre-intervention trends excluding 2009 deaths did not differ from control deaths (p=0.9).
source: The pre-intervention trends excluding 2009 deaths did not differ from control deaths (p=0.9).
evidence: Result from statistical comparison.

claim: Multilevel logistic regression was used to examine characteristics of health-seeking behavior associated with measles mortality.
source: We used multilevel logistic regression to examine characteristics of health-seeking behavior associated with measles mortality (Larsen and Merlo, 2005).
evidence: Description of analytical methods with citation to Larsen and Merlo, 2005.

claim: The data were organized into a three-level hierarchical structure consisting of children nested within districts nested within states.
source: We organized the data into a three-level hierarchical structure consisting of children (first level) nested within districts (second level) nested within states (third level).
evidence: Description of analytical methods.

claim: Random intercepts were fitted at the district and state level to account for regional variation.
source: We fitted random intercepts at the district and state level to account for regional variation.
evidence: Description of analytical methods.

claim: Coverage data were obtained from the District Level Household Surveys (2002–2004, 2007–2008 and 2011–2012) and National Family Health Surveys (2005–2006, and 2013–2014).
source: We obtained the coverage data from Indian national surveys corresponding to our study period including the Government of India's District Level Household Surveys (DLHS; 2002–2004, 2007–2008 and 2011–2012) and National Family Health Surveys (NFHS; 2005–2006, and 2013–2014).
evidence: Description of data sources.

claim: Maps were constructed using a generalized linear geostatistical model with integrated nested Laplace approximations.
source: We constructed maps of 1–59 month measles mortality to determine the geographical distribution of measles mortality risk in India. We fitted the data using a generalized linear geostatistical model with integrated nested Laplace approximations.
evidence: Description of analytical methods.

claim: R version 3.5.1 was used for mapping.
source: We used R version 3.5.1 for mapping.
evidence: Description of software used.

claim: Stata version 15 was used for statistical analysis.
source: We used Stata version 15 for statistical analysis.
evidence: Description of software used.
